reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Deficiency causes a bleeding tendency with a prolonged prothrombin time, and in more severe cases a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time
Newborns are especially vulnerable because of low placental transfer, immature gut flora, and low vitamin K content of breast milk, causing vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Routine neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, including its dangerous late intracranial form
In adults it results from fat malabsorption, biliary obstruction, prolonged antibiotic use, or poor intake, since much vitamin K also comes from gut bacteria
Warfarin acts by antagonising vitamin K, and its effect can be reversed by vitamin K when correction is needed
The coagulopathy corrects with vitamin K repletion, and rapid correction confirms the diagnosis
Because it is fat soluble, deficiency clusters with deficiencies of vitamins A, D, and E in malabsorptive states
reference.pathophysiology: Vitamin K is a cofactor for the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and on the anticoagulant proteins C and S, a modification required for their activity. Deficiency leaves these factors undercarboxylated and functionally inactive, impairing coagulation and producing bleeding. The vitamin is fat soluble and derives from dietary green vegetables and from synthesis by intestinal bacteria, so inadequate intake, fat malabsorption, absence of bile, and suppression of gut flora all reduce availability. Neonates start with low stores and sterile guts, explaining their particular susceptibility.
additionalDifferentials: Liver disease causing impaired synthesis of clotting factors
Other bleeding disorders such as thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time
Assessment of liver function to distinguish hepatic synthetic failure
Response of coagulation parameters to vitamin K repletion
Evaluation for fat malabsorption and biliary obstruction in adults
Consideration of coexisting fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies
redFlags: Active or severe bleeding, including gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Intracranial haemorrhage, especially late vitamin K deficiency bleeding in an infant
Coagulopathy in a patient requiring urgent surgery or intervention
Bleeding in the context of significant liver disease requiring broader management
reference.prognosis: Deficiency-related coagulopathy corrects reliably and rapidly with vitamin K when there is no severe liver disease; neonatal prophylaxis largely prevents the life-threatening bleeding of infancy.
pitfalls: Assuming a prolonged prothrombin time reflects liver disease when it is correctable vitamin K deficiency, or vice versa
Overlooking fat malabsorption or biliary obstruction as the underlying cause
Failing to ensure neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis
Not recognising coexisting deficiency of other fat-soluble vitamins
management: Repletion with vitamin K (phytomenadione), given orally in mild cases and parenterally when bleeding is significant
Fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate for active severe or life-threatening haemorrhage, giving immediate but temporary correction
Routine neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis at birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, including its late intracranial form
Treat the underlying cause such as fat malabsorption or biliary obstruction, and review prolonged antibiotic use
For warfarin-related over-anticoagulation with bleeding, reverse with vitamin K
Monitor prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time to confirm the rapid response that also verifies the diagnosis
